A bunch of people resist the notion because even after peer reviewed confirmation that the "drive" works, it is not readily explained. There were some notable people who came forward early on and stated unequivocally that it couldn't work because it breaks physics which is impossible, and admitting one was wrong - even in the face of mountains of data - is difficult for many people; it's a part of human nature that many people never get past.

The emdrive certainly challenges some of our previous understandings, but by definition it can't violate the laws of the universe. The best quote I heard on this topic went something like "Repeatable peer-reviewed scientific experiments producing an amazing and inexplicable result that are rejected in spite of the evidence in favor of past beliefs may not make sense from a standpoint of the scientific method, but in the context of history it is almost universally expected. All great leaps in scientific understanding have been resisted in the beginning by those who should have known better."

I think a lot of the resistance comes from a lack of understanding not only of the physics behind exactly what the emdrive is doing, but in the methodology involved in getting those results. Many people mistakenly believe this is a recent discovery, when in fact it is a decade old now! The first guy to discover it was a bit of a nut and refused to submit for peer review, and as they say extraordinary claims require extraordinary proof. It wasn't until a few years ago that a University in China was able to reproduce the drive and published their results for peer review. NASA's results are not a new experiment, they are a peer-review of China's results, modified from their data from the beginning to hopefully not only replicate the anomalous thrust readings, but also a higher level of efficiency... which they achieved on both counts. That was confirmation. Then NASA also tested the machine in vacuum to eliminate some other concerns about where the thrust might be coming from that could contaminate the results... and the drive still worked. Then Sonny White shined a laser through the drive's field while it was operating and got some potential FTL results... THOSE maybe FTL results are unverified, not yet peer reviewed, unproven, and interesting as hell. It's possible that the interesting and not peer-reviewer faster-than-light-maybe discovery has been twisted into a the-whole-thing-is-unverified myth by people who are unfamiliar with the experiment and what led up to these latest tests.
If something sounds too good to be true, it's not unreasonable to remain sceptical. It wouldn't be the first time peer reviewed result proving the impossible turned out to be impossible.

This particular technology has been around 14 years now, it hasn't been disproven in that time but has instead been confirmed many times, and instead is gaining steam now that Sonny White's team has been given free reign over Cannae's latest designs. I like where the momentum is going, at the very least. We may not understand exactly how it works, but the team publishing these latest results that have been grabbing headlines have a firm enough grasp to have improved efficiency based solely on China's published writings, and based on their own results have already stated they're confident in an order of magnitude greater efficiency in a next generation design. Even if the insanely weird faster-than-light observation was just an error (highly probable, and treated as such until a lot more than the one experiment says otherwise) electrical thrust generation that works in vacuum already has real world practical uses - even if the technology scales no more than we've already seen in action, it becomes a space drive that needs no fuel beyond a power source, something akin to NASA's ion drive. It could be adapted to a solar sail, or saddled to a nuclear reactor, and sent off on its merry way to explore the solar system for as long as that power source remains functional... and that's awesome.

It's definitely not "impossible" as the drives have been readily proven to work already... the difficult part is explaining why it does what it does; it's been many lifetimes since observational data was not readily explained by existing scientific knowledge, and that's why there has been resistance. Seperating the media's need to call it a "warp drive" or attribute scifi properties to it is probably where so much of the public skepticism comes from. Seperating that out is needed to understand the cutting edge science involved, and that is likely why no real info has been shared since the maybe-FTL test; conjecture only hurts the project.
